facts.statement: Baryonyx lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: Baryonyx () is a genus of theropod dinosaur which lived in the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous period, about 130–125 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first skeleton of Baryonyx was discovered in 1983 at the Smokejack Clay Pit in Surrey, England.
facts.quote: The first skeleton was discovered in 1983 in the Smokejack Clay Pit, of Surrey, England, in sediments of the Weald Clay Formation

facts.statement: Baryonyx was named by paleontologists Alan J. Charig and Angela C. Milner in 1986.
facts.quote: named by palaeontologists Alan J. Charig and Angela C. Milner in 1986

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Baryonyx was estimated to be between 7.5 and 10 meters long and weigh between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, which may not have been fully grown, was estimated to have been between 7.5 and 10 m long and to have weighed between 1.2 and 2 MT.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had robust forelimbs with a first-finger claw measuring approximately 31 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: It had robust forelimbs, with the eponymous first-finger claw measuring about 31 cm long.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur proven to be piscivorous, based on fish scales found in the stomach region of the holotype.
facts.quote: Baryonyx was the first theropod dinosaur demonstrated to have been piscivorous (fish-eating), as evidenced by fish scales in the stomach region of the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: Baryonyx may have been an active predator and scavenger, as evidenced by the presence of juvenile iguanodontian bones in its stomach.
facts.quote: It may also have been an active predator of larger prey and a scavenger, since it also contained bones of a juvenile iguanodontian.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Baryonyx may have had semi-aquatic habits.
facts.quote: Baryonyx may have had semi-aquatic habits

facts.statement: Baryonyx is now classified as a member of the family Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: Now recognised as a member of the family Spinosauridae, Baryonyx affinities were obscure when it was discovered.

facts.statement: The first remains of Baryonyx were found in January 1983 by amateur fossil collector William J. Walker.
facts.quote: In January 1983, the plumber and amateur fossil collector William J. Walker explored the Smokejack Clay Pit

facts.statement: Walker found the missing tip of the large claw after searching for an hour at the same site weeks later.
facts.quote: Walker returned to the same spot in the pit some weeks later, and found the missing part after searching for an hour.

facts.statement: It took six years of continuous preparation to extract all the bones from the rock matrix of the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: It took six years of almost constant preparation to get all the bones out of the rock

facts.statement: The holotype specimen represents approximately 65 percent of the complete skeleton.
facts.quote: The specimen represents about 65 per cent of the skeleton

facts.statement: Baryonyx was the first large Early Cretaceous theropod discovered anywhere in the world at the time of its finding.
facts.quote: Baryonyx was the first large Early Cretaceous theropod found anywhere in the world by that time.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was nicknamed "Claws" by journalists due to its large claws, a pun on the film Jaws.
facts.quote: Baryonyx was widely featured in international media, and was nicknamed "Claws" by journalists punning on the title of the film Jaws.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym of Baryonyx or if Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus.
facts.quote: Some researchers have suggested that Suchosaurus cultridens is a senior synonym (being an older name), and that Suchomimus tenerensis belongs in the same genus; subsequent authors have kept them separate.

facts.statement: In 1999, fossils from the Salas de los Infantes deposit in Spain were attributed to an immature Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 1999, a postorbital, squamosal, tooth, vertebral remains, metacarpals (hand bones), and a phalanx from the Salas de los Infantes deposit in Burgos Province, Spain, were attributed to an immature Baryonyx

facts.statement: In 2011, Octávio Mateus and colleagues attributed a nearly complete skeleton from Portugal to Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 2011, a specimen (catalogued as ML1190 in Museu da Lourinhã) from the Papo Seco Formation in Boca do Chapim, Portugal, with a fragmentary dentary, teeth, vertebrae, ribs, hip bones, a scapula, and a phalanx bone, was attributed to Baryonyx by the palaeontologist Octávio Mateus and colleagues

facts.statement: In 2019, researchers determined that a Portuguese skeleton previously assigned to Baryonyx did not belong to the genus because its dentary bone was not strongly upturned.
facts.quote: In 2019, the palaeontologist Thomas M. S. Arden and colleagues found that the Portuguese skeleton did not belong to Baryonyx, since the front of its dentary bone was not strongly upturned

facts.statement: In 2024, Erik Isasmendi and colleagues concluded that no spinosaurid fossils from Iberia could be assigned to Baryonyx.
facts.quote: A 2024 article by the palaeontologist Erik Isasmendi and colleagues reviewed the spinosaurid fossil record of Iberia and concluded that no specimens from there could be assigned to Baryonyx

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the species Suchosaurus cultridens in 1841 based on teeth found by Gideon A. Mantell in Tilgate Forest.
facts.quote: The type species of Suchosaurus, S. cultridens, was named by the biologist Richard Owen in 1841, based on teeth discovered by the geologist Gideon A. Mantell in Tilgate Forest

facts.statement: Henri Émile Sauvage named the species Suchosaurus girardi in 1897 based on fossils from Portugal.
facts.quote: A second species, S. girardi, was named by the palaeontologist Henri Émile Sauvage in 1897, based on jaw fragments and a tooth from Boca do Chapim, Portugal

facts.statement: In 1998, Philippe Taquet and Dale Russell named the genus and species Cristatusaurus lapparenti based on spinosaurid snouts from Niger.
facts.quote: In 1998, these fossils became the basis of the genus and species Cristatusaurus lapparenti, named by Taquet and the palaeontologist Dale Russell

facts.statement: In 2002, Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues proposed that Suchomimus tenerensis should be considered a species of Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 2002, the palaeontologist Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues proposed that Suchomimus tenerensis was similar enough to Baryonyx walkeri to be considered a species within the same genus

facts.statement: In 2007, Éric Buffetaut suggested that the teeth of Suchosaurus girardi were very similar to those of Baryonyx, differing only in stronger tooth crown flutes.
facts.quote: In 2007, the palaeontologist Éric Buffetaut considered the teeth of S. girardi very similar to those of Baryonyx (and S. cultridens) except for the stronger development of the tooth crown flutes

facts.statement: In 2011, Mateus and colleagues considered the species of Suchosaurus to be nomina dubia despite their close relationship to Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 2011, Mateus and colleagues agreed that Suchosaurus was closely related to Baryonyx, but considered both species in the former genus nomina dubia

facts.statement: In 2026, Frédéric Pittet found that Cristatusaurus and Suchomimus share a premaxillary crest not found in Baryonyx, suggesting they are distinct from Baryonyx.
facts.quote: In 2026, the palaeontologist Frédéric Pittet found that assigned specimens of Cristatusaurus and Suchomimus shared features such as a crest on the premaxilla not found in Baryonyx

facts.statement: Baryonyx is estimated to have been 7.5 to 10 meters long, 2.5 meters tall at the hip, and weighed between 1.2 and 2 metric tons.
facts.quote: Baryonyx is estimated to have been between 7.5 and 10 m long, 2.5 m in hip height, and to have weighed between 1.2 and 2 MT

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Baryonyx walkeri shows unfused skull and vertebrae elements, suggesting the individual was not fully grown.
facts.quote: The fact that elements of the skull and vertebral column of the B. walkeri holotype specimen (NHM R9951) do not appear to have co-ossified (fused) suggests that the individual was not fully grown

facts.statement: The fused sternum of the holotype specimen suggests that the individual may have been mature.
facts.quote: On the other hand, the specimen's fused sternum indicates that it may have been mature

facts.statement: Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues raised the possibility in 2004 that a maxilla fragment from Spain belonged to Suchomimus rather than Baryonyx.
facts.quote: although the palaeontologist Thomas R. Holtz and colleagues raised the possibility that it could have belonged to Suchomimus in 2004

facts.statement: Barker and colleagues stated that the description of new genera from the Wessex Formation makes the presence of Baryonyx in that formation ambiguous.
facts.quote: Barker and colleagues stated that the recognition of the Wessex Formation specimens as new genera renders the presence of Baryonyx there ambiguous

facts.statement: In 2003, Milner concurred that spinosaurid material from Niger was indistinguishable from Baryonyx.
facts.quote: Milner concurred that the material from Niger was indistinguishable from Baryonyx in 2003

facts.statement: In 2021, Barker and colleagues found that Suchomimus is more closely related to the British genera Riparovenator and Ceratosuchops than to Baryonyx.
facts.quote: Barker and colleagues found Suchomimus to be closer related to the British genera Riparovenator and Ceratosuchops than to Baryonyx in 2021

facts.statement: The skull of Baryonyx was estimated to be 91 to 95 centimeters long based on comparisons with the larger genus Suchomimus.
facts.quote: The full length of the skull is estimated to have been 91 - 95 cm long, based on comparison with that of the related genus Suchomimus (which was 20% larger).

facts.statement: Baryonyx had fused nasal bones and a sagittal crest above the eyes, distinguishing it from other spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The nasal bones were fused, which distinguished Baryonyx from other spinosaurids, and a sagittal crest was present above the eyes, on the upper mid-line of the nasals.

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone formed a solid, almost triangular horn core in front of the eye, distinct from other spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The lacrimal bone in front of the eye appears to have formed a horn core similar to those seen, for example, in Allosaurus, and was distinct from other spinosaurids in being solid and almost triangular.

facts.statement: The teeth had around six to eight denticles per millimeter, a much higher number than in large theropods like Torvosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: There were around six to eight denticles per mm (0.039 in), a much larger number than in large-bodied theropods like Torvosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: The first finger of the holotype specimen bore a large claw measuring about 31 centimeters along its curve.
facts.quote: The first finger bore a large claw measuring about 31 cm along its curve in the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was unique among spinosaurids for having a marked side-to-side constriction in a vertebra belonging to the sacrum or front of the tail.
facts.quote: Baryonyx was unique among spinosaurids in having a marked constriction from side to side in a vertebra that either belonged to the sacrum or front of the tail.

facts.statement: The coracoid connected with the scapula in a unique peg-and-notch articulation found only among spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The coracoid tapered hind-wards when viewed in profile, and, uniquely among spinosaurids, connected with the scapula in a peg-and-notch articulation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that some cranial bones were misidentified, leading to an occiput reconstructed as too deep, and propose the skull was actually as low, long, and narrow as that of Suchomimus.
facts.quote: Sereno and colleagues suggested that some of Baryonyx cranial bones had been misidentified by Charig and Milner, resulting in the occiput being reconstructed as too deep, and that the skull was instead probably as low, long and narrow as that of Suchomimus.

facts.statement: Researchers originally classified Baryonyx in its own family, Baryonychidae, because it was considered unique among theropods.
facts.quote: In their original description, Charig and Milner found Baryonyx unique enough to warrant a new family of theropod dinosaurs: Baryonychidae.

facts.statement: In 2004, Holtz and colleagues classified the family Baryonychidae as a synonym of Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: Holtz and colleagues listed Baryonychidae as a synonym of Spinosauridae in 2004.

facts.statement: The subfamily Baryonychinae was distinguished by small size, a larger number of teeth behind the snout tip, deeply keeled front vertebrae, and serrated teeth.
facts.quote: Baryonychinae was distinguished by the small size and larger number of teeth in the dentary behind the terminal rosette, the deeply keeled front dorsal vertebrae, and by having serrated teeth.

facts.statement: A 2017 study suggested the clade Baryonychinae was not well supported because serrated teeth might be an ancestral trait shared by all spinosaurids.
facts.quote: A 2017 study by the palaeontologists Marcos A. F. Sales and Cesar L. Schultz found that the clade Baryonychinae was not well supported, since serrated teeth may be an ancestral trait among spinosaurids.

facts.statement: Unlike crocodiles, the body skeletons of Baryonyx and its relatives do not show clear adaptations for an aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Unlike crocodiles, the post-cranial skeletons of baryonychine spinosaurids do not appear to have aquatic adaptations.

facts.statement: In 2002, Buffetaut and Ouaja suggested that Baryonyx ancestors gave rise to Spinosaurinae, which later replaced them in Africa.
facts.quote: Buffetaut and the Tunisian palaeontologist Mohamed Ouaja also suggested in 2002 that baryonychines could be the ancestors of spinosaurines, which appear to have replaced the former in Africa.

facts.statement: In 2003, Milner suggested spinosaurids originated in Laurasia during the Jurassic and spread to Gondwana via the Iberian land bridge.
facts.quote: Milner suggested in 2003 that spinosaurids originated in Laurasia during the Jurassic, and dispersed via the Iberian land bridge into Gondwana, where they radiated.

facts.statement: The exact direction of spinosaurid dispersal between Europe and Africa remains unknown, with new finds in Asia and Australia suggesting a complex migration history.
facts.quote: The direction of the dispersal between Europe and Africa is still unknown, and subsequent discoveries of spinosaurid remains in Asia and possibly Australia indicate that it may have been complex.

facts.statement: In 2020, researchers stated that Baryonyx is the oldest confirmed spinosaurid, though older fossils have been tentatively assigned to the group.
facts.quote: Malafaia and colleagues stated in 2020 that Baryonyx remains the oldest unquestionable spinosaurid, while acknowledging that older remains had also been tentatively assigned to the group.

facts.statement: In 2021, Barker and colleagues supported a European origin for spinosaurids that expanded to Asia and Gondwana in the early Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Barker and colleagues found support for a European origin for spinosaurids in 2021, with an expansion to Asia and Gondwana during the first half of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggested in contrast to Sereno that there were at least two separate dispersal events from Europe to Africa for spinosaurids.
facts.quote: In contrast to Sereno, these authors suggested there had been at least two dispersal events from Europe to Africa, leading to Suchomimus and the African part of Spinosaurinae.

facts.statement: In 1986, researchers suggested Baryonyx was a fish-eater that crouched on riverbanks to use its claw to spear fish like a grizzly bear.
facts.quote: In 1986, Charig and Milner suggested that its elongated snout with many finely serrated teeth indicated that Baryonyx was piscivorous (fish-eating), speculating that it crouched on a riverbank and used its claw to gaff fish out of the water (similar to the modern grizzly bear).

facts.statement: In 1997, Charig and Milner found the first evidence of fish-eating in a theropod dinosaur in the stomach of a Baryonyx specimen, which contained fish scales, teeth, and iguanodontian bones.
facts.quote: In 1997, Charig and Milner demonstrated direct dietary evidence in the stomach region of the B. walkeri holotype. It contained the first evidence of piscivory in a theropod dinosaur, acid-etched scales and teeth of the common fish Scheenstia mantelli (then classified in the genus Lepidotes), and abraded or etched bones of a young iguanodontian.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had crocodile-like adaptations including long narrow jaws with a terminal rosette and a snout with a downturned tip and notch, suggesting it caught and swallowed prey like a gharial.
facts.quote: They also presented circumstantial evidence for piscivory, such as crocodile-like adaptations for catching and swallowing prey: long, narrow jaws with their "terminal rosette", similar to those of a gharial, and the downturned tip and notch of the snout.

facts.statement: An apparent gizzard stone was found with the Baryonyx holotype specimen.
facts.quote: An apparent gastrolith (gizzard stone) was also found with the specimen.

facts.statement: A 2004 discovery of a spinosaurid tooth embedded in a pterosaur neck vertebra suggested spinosaurids were not exclusively fish-eaters.
facts.quote: In 2004, a pterosaur neck vertebra from Brazil with a spinosaurid tooth embedded in it reported by Buffetaut and colleagues confirmed that the latter were not exclusively piscivorous.

facts.statement: A 2007 study found Baryonyx's snout biomechanics were most similar to a gharial, supporting a piscivorous diet for spinosaurids.
facts.quote: A 2007 finite element analysis of CT scanned snouts by the palaeontologist Emily J. Rayfield and colleagues indicated that the biomechanics of Baryonyx were most similar to those of the gharial and unlike those of the American alligator and more-conventional theropods, supporting a piscivorous diet for spinosaurids.

facts.statement: A 2013 study concluded Baryonyx performed differently than a gharial, suggesting spinosaurids were not exclusive fish-eaters and their diet depended on their size.
facts.quote: A 2013 beam-theory study by the palaeontologists Andrew R. Cuff and Rayfield compared the biomechanics of CT-scanned spinosaurid snouts with those of extant crocodilians, and found the snouts of Baryonyx and Spinosaurus similar in their resistance to bending and torsion. Baryonyx was found to have relatively high resistance in the snout to dorsoventral bending compared with Spinosaurus and the gharial. The authors concluded (in contrast to the 2007 study) that Baryonyx performed differently than the gharial; spinosaurids were not exclusive piscivores, and their diet was determined by their individual size.

facts.statement: In 2014, researchers ruled out that Baryonyx gaffed fish out of the water or darted its head like a heron because its neck was not S-curved and its eyes were not positioned for binocular vision.
facts.quote: In a 2014 conference abstract, the palaeontologist Danny Anduza and Fowler pointed out that grizzly bears do not gaff fish out of the water as was suggested for Baryonyx, and also ruled out that the dinosaur would not have darted its head like herons, since the necks of spinosaurids were not strongly S-curved, and their eyes were not well-positioned for binocular vision.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Baryonyx caught fish with sideways jaw sweeps and used its claws to stamp down and impale large fish, similar to grizzly bears and fishing cats.
facts.quote: Instead, they suggested the jaws would have made sideways sweeps to catch fish, like the gharial, with the hand claws probably used to stamp down and impale large fish, whereafter they manipulated them with their jaws, in a manner similar to grizzly bears and fishing cats.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found adult spinosaurs could move the halves of their lower jaw sideways to widen the throat opening, allowing them to swallow large prey.
facts.quote: A 2016 study by the palaeontologist Christophe Hendrickx and colleagues found that adult spinosaurs could displace their mandibular rami (halves of the lower jaw) sideways when the jaw was depressed, which allowed the pharynx (opening that connects the mouth to the oesophagus) to be widened.

facts.statement: Portuguese Baryonyx fossils found with isolated iguanodontian teeth support the idea that spinosaurs were opportunistic feeders.
facts.quote: They also reported that some possible Portuguese Baryonyx fossils were found associated with isolated iguanodontian teeth, and listed it along with other such associations as support for opportunistic feeding behaviour in spinosaurs.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found spinosaurid jaws were convergent with pike conger eels, which have side-compressed jaws, elongated snouts with a terminal rosette, and a notch with smaller teeth.
facts.quote: Another 2016 study by the palaeontologist Romain Vullo and colleagues found that the jaws of spinosaurids were convergent with those of pike conger eels; these fish also have jaws that are compressed side to side (whereas the jaws of crocodilians are compressed from top to bottom), an elongated snout with a "terminal rosette" that bears enlarged teeth, and a notch behind the rosette with smaller teeth.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest spinosaurid jaws evolved to grab prey in low-light aquatic environments and may have aided in prey detection.
facts.quote: Such jaws likely evolved for grabbing prey in aquatic environments with low light, and may have helped in prey detection.

facts.statement: A 2023 study found the brain anatomy of Baryonyx was similar to other non-maniraptoriform theropods.
facts.quote: A 2023 study by Barker and colleagues based on CT scans of the braincases of Baryonyx and Ceratosuchops found that the brain anatomy of these baryonychines was similar to that of other non-maniraptoriform theropods.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had unexceptional hearing and smell, and less developed gaze stabilization than spinosaurines, suggesting its behavior was similar to other large terrestrial theropods.
facts.quote: Their neurosensory capabilities such as hearing and olfaction (sense of smell) were unexceptional, and their gaze stabilisation less developed than those of spinosaurines, so their behavioural adaptations were probably comparable to those of other large-bodied terrestrial theropods.

facts.statement: The original describers Charig and Milner did not consider Baryonyx to be an aquatic animal.
facts.quote: In their original description, Charig and Milner did not consider Baryonyx to be aquatic

facts.statement: Researchers speculated that Baryonyx's elongated skull, long neck, and strong humerus indicated it was a facultative quadruped, a trait unique among theropods.
facts.quote: They speculated that the elongated skull, long neck, and strong humerus of Baryonyx indicated that the animal was a facultative quadruped, unique among theropods

facts.statement: Paleontologists Hone and Holtz suggested that spinosaurid forelimbs were not optimal for trapping prey but appeared similar to those of digging animals.
facts.quote: Hone and Holtz furthermore suggested that the forelimbs of spinosaurids do not seem optimal for trapping prey, but instead appear similar to the forelimbs of digging animals

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the ability to dig in spinosaurids would have been useful for excavating nests, digging for water, or reaching certain types of prey.
facts.quote: They suggested that the ability to dig would have been useful when excavating nests, digging for water, or to reach some kinds of prey

facts.statement: Authors proposed that submersion in water served as thermoregulation for spinosaurids, similar to crocodiles and hippopotamuses, despite a lack of specific aquatic anatomical adaptations.
facts.quote: Since most spinosaurids do not appear to have anatomical adaptations for an aquatic lifestyle, the authors proposed that submersion in water was a means of thermoregulation similar to that of crocodiles and hippopotamuses

facts.statement: Researchers suggested spinosaurids may have adopted aquatic habitats and a fish-based diet to avoid competition with large terrestrial theropods.
facts.quote: Spinosaurids may also have turned to aquatic habitats and piscivory to avoid competition with large, more-terrestrial theropods

facts.statement: A 2016 statistical study by Sales and colleagues concluded that spinosaurids had the strongest association with coastal paleoenvironments.
facts.quote: In 2016, Sales and colleagues statistically examined the fossil distribution of spinosaurids, abelisaurids, and carcharodontosaurids, and concluded that spinosaurids had the strongest support for association with coastal palaeoenvironments

facts.statement: Spinosaurids inhabited inland environments comparable to carcharodontosaurids, suggesting they may have been more generalist than previously thought.
facts.quote: Spinosaurids also appear to have inhabited inland environments (with their distribution there being comparable to carcharodontosaurids), which indicates they may have been more generalist than usually thought

facts.statement: Smaller nostrils in some spinosaurids suggest lesser olfactory abilities compared to modern piscivorous animals, implying they may have relied on vision and mechanoreception when hunting fish.
facts.quote: As some spinosaurids have smaller nostrils than others, their olfactory abilities were presumably lesser, as in modern piscivorous animals, and they may instead have used other senses (such as vision and mechanoreception) when hunting fish

facts.statement: The Weald Clay Formation, where Baryonyx was found, dates from the Hauterivian to Barremian ages, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Weald Clay Formation consists of sediments of Hauterivian (Lower Weald Clay) to Barremian (Upper Weald Clay) age, about 130–125 million years old

facts.statement: The original Baryonyx specimen was found in clay representing a non-marine still water environment interpreted as fluvial or mudflat areas with shallow water, lagoons, and marshes.
facts.quote: The original Baryonyx specimen was found in the latter, in clay representing non-marine still water, which has been interpreted as a fluvial or mudflat environment with shallow water, lagoons, and marshes

facts.statement: Dinosaurs found at the Baryonyx locality include the ornithopods Mantellisaurus and Paludohadros, as well as small sauropods.
facts.quote: Dinosaurs from the locality include the ornithopods Mantellisaurus, Paludohadros, and small sauropods

facts.statement: Other vertebrates found in the Weald Clay include crocodiles, pterosaurs, lizards like Dorsetisaurus, amphibians, sharks like Hybodus, and bony fishes including Scheenstia.
facts.quote: Other vertebrates from the Weald Clay include crocodiles, pterosaurs, lizards (such as Dorsetisaurus), amphibians, sharks (such as Hybodus), and bony fishes (including Scheenstia)

facts.statement: Other invertebrates found in the Weald Clay include ostracods, isopods, conchostracans, and bivalves.
facts.quote: Other invertebrates include ostracods, isopods, conchostracans, and bivalves

facts.statement: The plants Weichselia and the aquatic, herbaceous Bevhalstia were common in the Weald Clay environment.
facts.quote: The plants Weichselia and the aquatic, herbaceous Bevhalstia were common

facts.statement: Other plants found in the Weald Clay include ferns, horsetails, club mosses, and conifers.
facts.quote: Other plants found include ferns, horsetails, club mosses, and conifers

facts.statement: Other dinosaurs from the Wessex Formation include the ornithopods Brighstoneus, Hypsilophodon, and Valdosaurus; the sauropods Ornithopsis, Eucamerotus, and Chondrosteosaurus; and the ankylosaur Polacanthus.
facts.quote: the ornithopods Brighstoneus, Hypsilophodon, and Valdosaurus; the sauropods Ornithopsis, Eucamerotus, and Chondrosteosaurus; and the ankylosaur Polacanthus

facts.statement: Researchers Charig and Milner proposed a scenario to explain the fossilization process of the Baryonyx walkeri holotype.
facts.quote: Charig and Milner presented a possible scenario explaining the taphonomy (changes during decay and fossilisation) of the B. walkeri holotype specimen.

facts.statement: The environment where the holotype died was likely suitable for a fish-eating animal.
facts.quote: The area where the specimen died seems to have been suitable for a piscivorous animal.

facts.statement: Baryonyx likely caught fish and scavenged on mud plains, possibly becoming trapped in mud before dying.
facts.quote: It may have caught fish and scavenged on the mud plain, becoming mired before it died and was buried.

facts.statement: The lack of gnaw marks on the well-preserved bones suggests the carcass was quickly buried by sediment, avoiding scavengers.
facts.quote: Since the bones are well-preserved and had no gnaw marks, the carcass appears to have been undisturbed by scavengers (suggesting that it was quickly covered by sediment).

facts.statement: Some bones, including the dentary and ribs, were likely broken by trampling from large animals while buried.
facts.quote: The girdle and limb bones, the dentary, and a rib were broken before fossilisation, perhaps from trampling by large animals while buried.

facts.statement: Most of the tail was likely lost before fossilization due to scavenging or rotting and floating away.
facts.quote: Most of the tail appears to have been lost before fossilisation, perhaps due to scavenging, or having rotted and floated off.

facts.statement: The carcass likely lay on its back, which may explain why lower teeth fell out while some upper teeth remained in their sockets.
facts.quote: The orientation of the bones indicates that the carcass lay on its back (perhaps tilted slightly to the left, with the right side upwards), which may explain why all the lower teeth had fallen out of their sockets and some upper teeth were still in place.

facts.statement: The genus Baryonyx was named by Charig and Milner in 1987.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Charig & Milner, 1987

facts.statement: The species Baryonyx walkeri was named by Charig and Milner in 1987.
facts.quote: species_authority: Charig & Milner, 1987

facts.statement: Baryonyx lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 130 to 125 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 130 y 125 millones de años durante el Aptiense, en lo que es hoy Europa.

facts.statement: The first specimen of Baryonyx was found in England.
facts.quote: El primer ejemplar fue encontrado en Inglaterra.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was a large predator measuring about 9.75 meters in length, 2.55 meters in hip height, and weighing between 1.7 and 2.7 tons.
facts.quote: Baryonyx era un predador de gran tamaño que midió unos 9.75 metros de longitud, 2.55 de altura a la cadera y entre 1.7 y 2.7 toneladas

facts.statement: The holotype's unfused skull and vertebrae suggest it was not fully grown, and adults may have been larger, similar to Spinosaurus which reached 15 meters and 10 tons.
facts.quote: El hecho que los elementos del cráneo y la columna vertebral del espécimen holotipo de B. walkeri, NHM R9951, no parecen haber estado fusionados, lo que sugiere que el individuo no estaba completamente crecido, y el animal maduro pudo haber sido más grande, como sucede en el relacionado Spinosaurus, que alcanzó 15 metros de largo y 10 toneladas.

facts.statement: Baryonyx was an unusual theropod whose pelvic structure suggests it was bipedal when moving.
facts.quote: Baryonyx es un terópodo muy inusual. La estructura de su pelvis sugiere que era bípedo cuando se desplazaba de un lugar a otro.

facts.statement: Like dromaeosaurids, Baryonyx had large curved claws about 35 centimeters long, but these were located on its hands rather than its feet.
facts.quote: Al igual que los dromeosáuridos, Baryonyx tenía un par de grandes garras curvas, de alrededor de 35 centímetros, pero al contrario que éstos, no se situaba en los pies, sino en las manos.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a long neck that was very inflexible and lacked the S-shape seen in many other theropods.
facts.quote: El largo cuello era muy poco flexible y no tenía la forma en S de muchos otros terópodos.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had large, uniquely crocodilian-looking jaws with 96 teeth, double the number of most of its relatives.
facts.quote: Las grandes mandíbulas eran singularmente cocodrilianas en aspecto y tenían 96 dientes, el doble que la mayoría de sus parientes.

facts.statement: It is possible that Baryonyx's snout featured a small crest.
facts.quote: Es posible que el hocico presentase una pequeña cresta.

facts.statement: The upper jaw had an acute angle near the snout, a feature seen in crocodiles that helps prevent prey from escaping.
facts.quote: La mandíbula superior tenía un ángulo agudo cerca del hocico, una característica vista en cocodrilos que ayuda a evitar que la presa se escape.

facts.statement: The total skull length is estimated at 950 millimeters, based on comparison with the related genus Suchomimus, which is 20% larger.
facts.quote: La longitud total del cráneo se ha estimado en 950 milímetros, basado en la comparación con la del género relacionado Suchomimus, que es 20% más grande.

facts.statement: The front of the snout, 130 millimeters long, was spatula-shaped like the modern gharial, a feature called a "rosette snout," while the front of the lower margin, 70 millimeters long, curved downward.
facts.quote: El frente del hocico de 130 milímetros estaba ampliado en forma de espátula, de forma similar al moderno gavial , lo que se llama "hocico en roseta" y el frente del margen inferior de 70 milímetros se curvaba hacia abajo.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a rudimentary secondary palate similar to crocodiles, unlike most theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Baryonyx tenía un paladar secundario rudimentario, similar a los cocodrilos, pero a diferencia de la mayoría de los dinosaurios terópodos.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a sagittal crest above the eyes on the midline of the nasal bones that was triangular, narrow, and sharp at the front.
facts.quote: Tenía una cresta sagital por encima de los ojos, en la línea media superior de los huesos nasales , que era triangular, estrecha y afilada en el frente.

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone in front of the eye appears to have formed a horn core similar to that seen in Allosaurus.
facts.quote: El hueso lagrimal en frente del ojo parece haber formado un núcleo de un cuerno similar al visto, por ejemplo, en Allosaurus.

facts.statement: The teeth were shaped like recurved cones, slightly flattened on the side.
facts.quote: Los dientes tenían la forma de conos recurvados, algo aplanados de lado.

facts.statement: There were seven narrow, uniform serrations per millimeter, more than in most theropods.
facts.quote: Había siete dentículos estrechos y uniformes por milímetro, más que en la mayoría de los terópodos.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that some Baryonyx cranial bones were misidentified, leading to an overly deep occipital in reconstructions, and the skull was likely as low, long, and narrow as its close relative Suchomimus.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que algunos de los huesos craneales de Baryonyx han sido mal identificados resultando en un occipital demasiado profundo en la reconstrucción y el cráneo fue probablemente tan bajo, largo y estrecho como en su pariente cercano, Suchomimus.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a nearly straight S-shaped neck, differing from the typical S-curve seen in other theropods.
facts.quote: El cuello formaba una forma de sigmoidea más recta, con una menor típica forma de S que la observada en otros terópodos.

facts.statement: Like other dinosaurs, Baryonyx reduced its body weight using fenestrae (openings) in the neural arches and pleurocoels (hollow depressions) near the transverse processes.
facts.quote: Al igual que otros dinosaurios, Baryonyx redujo su peso con fenestras, aberturas en el hueso, en los arcos neurales y con pleurocoelos, depresiones huecas, en el cuerpo, principalmente cerca de los procesos transversales.

facts.statement: Baryonyx had a short, robust humerus with expanded, flattened ends that formed the top of the deltopectoral crest, a muscle anchor area.
facts.quote: El húmero era corto y robusto, con sus extremos amplios expandidos y aplanados formando la parte superior de la cresta deltopectoral, la zona de anclaje muscular y porción la inferior para la articulación con el radio y el cúbito.

facts.statement: According to a 2021 analysis by Barker and colleagues, Baryonyx is classified within the family Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: El cladograma siguiente muestra la posición de Baryonyx dentro de Spinosauridae, según Barker y colegas, 2021.

facts.statement: Baryonyx belongs to the subfamily Baryonychinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Baryonychinae

facts.statement: Baryonyx is a member of the family Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Spinosauridae

facts.statement: Baryonyx lived between 139.1 and 110.1 million years ago, during the Berriasian to Albian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Berriasian to Albian (139.1 to 110.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The genus Baryonyx was named by Charig and Milner in 1986.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Baryonyx (genus), Charig and Milner 1986

facts.statement: The first evidence of a piscivorous diet in a theropod dinosaur included stomach contents of the fish Scheenstia mantelli (formerly Lepidotes) and bones of a young Iguanodon.
facts.quote: La primera evidencia de dieta piscívora en un dinosaurio terópodo son escamas dañada por el ácido estomacal y dientes del común pescado Scheenstia mantelli, clasificado entonces en el género Lepidotes, y restos de huesos de un Iguanodon joven.

facts.statement: In 1987, Andrew Kitchener disputed the piscivorous behavior of Baryonyx, suggesting it was a scavenger that used its long neck to feed on the ground and its claws to rip into carcasses.
facts.quote: En 1987 Andrew Kitchener disputó el comportamiento piscívoro de Baryonyx y sugirió que habría sido un carroñero, usando su largo cuello para alimentarse en el suelo, sus garras para romper en un cadáver, y su hocico largo, con fosas nasales lejos para respirar, para investigar la cavidad del cuerpo.

facts.statement: Kitchener argued that Baryonyx's jaws and teeth were too weak to kill other dinosaurs and too heavy to catch fish, possessing too many adaptations for scavenging.
facts.quote: Kitchener argumentó que las mandíbulas y los dientes de Baryonyx eran demasiado débiles para matar a otros dinosaurios y demasiado pesados para capturar peces, con demasiadas adaptaciones para pescar.

facts.statement: A 2004 discovery of a spinosaurid tooth embedded in a Brazilian pterosaur vertebra confirmed that spinosaurids were not exclusively piscivorous.
facts.quote: En 2004, una vértebra del cuello de un pterosaurio de Brasil con un diente de un espinosáurido incrustado en ella confirmó que estos últimos no eran exclusivamente piscívoros.

facts.statement: A 2013 study concluded that Baryonyx functioned differently than a gharial, having relatively high resistance to dorsoventral flexion compared to Spinosaurus and the gharial, contrasting with a 2007 study.
facts.quote: Un estudio de la teoría del haz de 2013 comparó la biomecánica de los hocicos de espinosáuridos escaneados por CT con los de los cocodrilos existentes y encontró los hocicos de Baryonyx y Spinosaurus similares en su resistencia a la flexión y torsión. Se encontró que Baryonyx tenía relativamente alta resistencia en el hocico a la flexión dorsoventral en comparación con Spinosaurus y el gavial. Los autores concluyeron, en contraste con el estudio de 2007, que Baryonyx funcionaba de manera diferente que el gavial.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found that spinosaurid jaws were convergent with those of the pike fish (lucio).
facts.quote: Otro estudio de 2016 encontró que las mandíbulas de los espinosáuridos eran convergentes con las de los lucio.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found that adult spinosaurids could laterally displace their lower jaw halves when the jaw was depressed, allowing them to widen the pharynx to swallow large prey.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 2016 encontró que los espinosáuridos adultos podrían desplazar lateralmente sus ramas mandibulares, mitades de la mandíbula inferior, cuando la mandíbula estaba deprimida, lo que permitió ampliar la faringe, abertura que conduce de la garganta al estómago.
